datasets.title: Lawyer advertising rules by state (50 states and DC)
datasets.summary: The lawyer advertising rules of every US state and DC, in plain English: ad filing, what each ad must include, waiting periods for injury contact, claims and testimonials, referral and lead rules, ads in other languages, call-recording consent, texting law and privacy law, plus state laws on drug and medical-device ads. datasets.measurementTechnique: Each cell summarizes the jurisdiction’s rule in plain English from its rules of professional conduct as published by its high court or official bar, official ethics opinions and the official statute site. A cell is marked P when every fact in it is quoted word for word from that official text, D when the state’s own text could not be read at an official source (the cell says why, and the ABA Model Rule is assumed), and U when the question is open; each source carries the date it was read.

datasets.title: Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts
datasets.summary: How many lawyers each bar counts in each county, for seven states. Ohio: attorneys by county of address and status, from the Supreme Court of Ohio's attorney directory list (88 counties, with admission decade, private practice and Spanish speakers). California: active, inactive, judge and not-eligible licensees in each of the 58 counties, from the State Bar's county table. Michigan: active State Bar members living in each of the 83 counties, with private practice and the change from 2024. Idaho: members by status in each of the seven judicial districts. Arizona: active State Bar members in each of the 15 counties (the Bar's 2022 report). Washington: WSBA licensees of every type (lawyers plus limited licensees) in each of the 39 counties, with the attorney counts by member type. Pennsylvania: active attorneys in the seven counties the Disciplinary Board's annual report lists, and the Board's statewide status counts. Each record carries the source's own as-of date and a rate per 10,000 residents from the Census Bureau's county estimate. Only counts are published, and where a count is built from a directory file no name, birthdate, address or registration number is kept or written. In Ohio, counts of one to four in a disciplinary, deceased or other status, an admission decade, private practice or Spanish are withheld, and where a withheld count could be worked out from a county's total or the statewide figures, another count in the same group is withheld too. Every state record ties to its source's own total, and every published number is read a second time from the source file before release.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many lawyers already serve a county before choosing where to advertise: active attorneys per 10,000 residents, how many are inactive or retired, and for some states how many are in private practice or admitted recently. The seven bars count differently: the unit of each record is printed with it (active attorneys with an address in the county, active members living in the county, or all members of every license type), the as-of date differs by state and a county is where the lawyer's address is, not where clients live. Compare counties within a state, not one state's count with another's.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23777037, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Attorneys by county in Ohio, California, Michigan, Idaho, Arizona, Washington and Pennsylvania, from each bar's public counts (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23777037
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of lawyers from state bars' and courts' public count pages, reports and directory, kept for research and marketing planning. A status is the bar's record, not a judgment of any lawyer's skill or standing, and a county is the county of the address the lawyer gave, not where the lawyer practices or where clients live. Rights and deadlines in a matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts)
datasets.summary: Bankruptcy cases commenced in the 12 months ending on each quarter-end, from the U.S. Courts' Tables F-5A (by county and chapter), F-2 (by court district, chapter and business or nonbusiness debt) and F (cases filed, terminated and pending). One record per area: the United States, every state, DC and territory, 93 court districts and about 3,100 counties. Each gives the latest period's cases by Chapter 7, 11, 13 and other chapters, the business and nonbusiness split, the change on the year before, filings per 1,000 residents (Census 2025 population estimates) and the court's figures for the six earlier periods. Every table is checked against the court's own totals row. Counts of cases, not outcomes: a filing is not a discharge.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where debt trouble reaches the federal bankruptcy courts, how Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 mix in a state or county, and which districts are growing, before you size a bankruptcy practice's market. It counts cases commenced, not people helped or fees earned.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23739952, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts from the courts' published statistics, kept for marketing planning. A filing is not a discharge or an outcome, and the courts revise the tables as their database updates; check the current table at uscourts.gov.

datasets.title: The new-lawyer pipeline by jurisdiction: bar exam pass rates and new admissions, 2025
datasets.summary: For every US jurisdiction that reports to the National Conference of Bar Examiners (the 50 states, DC, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands): the overall 2025 bar exam pass rate, how many new lawyers were admitted in 2025 (by examination, by transferred UBE score and on motion), how admissions by exam or transferred score changed since 2021, and how much of the total came from transferred scores and from motion. NCBE reserves its published tables, so this dataset republishes none of them: every figure is one we derive from them (a rate, a sum, a change, a share), credited to NCBE with a link to the table it comes from. Each jurisdiction's rows add up to NCBE's own totals row before anything is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the new-lawyer market in a state: how many people are licensed each year, how many arrive by passing the exam, by moving a score or by moving their license, and whether that supply is growing. A state with a falling count and a low pass rate is losing new lawyers to its neighbours. Read it beside the lawyer wages and law-offices datasets before you decide where to recruit or advertise to new lawyers.

datasets.title: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026
datasets.summary: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026: aggregated, rounded, and small groups suppressed. Our data on law-firm marketing, shown as bands, named tiers and rounded values, one table per file. The public tables cover how quickly inquiries become signed clients, phone calls and signed clients, AI answers and organic search clicks, search-ad click costs, what people type, calls from ads, Local Services Ads leads, inquiries by quarter and ad cost per signed client. Each row gives the measure, the band or tier, its unit and a rough size band. Every value is aggregated across many observations; values resting on too few observations, or resting mostly on a few, are suppressed for privacy. Values are approximate, so read the band, not a point. The methods page defines every measure and the protection steps.
datasets.uses: Use it to compare your own firm's figure with a band, not to predict a result: a band is a range and a tier is a named range, so a firm above or below it is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a problem.

datasets.title: New business applications by county (Census Business Formation Statistics)
datasets.summary: Business applications (requests for a new Employer Identification Number) in every U.S. county from 2005 to 2025, with each county's latest count, the change over a year and since 2019, and the sums for each state and the nation, from the Census Bureau's Business Formation Statistics annual county file. The Census Bureau applied differentially private noise to the June 2026 release, so every record is flagged noise; county sums are checked against the Bureau's own monthly state series.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where new businesses are being started: which counties take in the most new-business applications, how fast that is growing, and how a county compares with its state. datasets.title: California court filings by county: civil, criminal, family, juvenile, probate and appeals, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25
datasets.summary: How many cases were filed in each of California's 58 superior courts (one per county) and statewide, by case type, from the Judicial Council of California's Court Statistics Reports: unlimited civil (motor-vehicle injury, other injury and wrongful death, other civil), limited civil, unlawful detainer, small claims, felonies and misdemeanors, family law, juvenile, probate, mental health and appeals. One record per county and case type, with the prior year beside it. In every table the 58 counties add up exactly to the report's own statewide row, and the totals inside each row add up too. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is. A filing is a new case opened in the county's superior court, so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Filings are for a state fiscal year (July 1 to June 30). Compare a county's count with the statewide row and with the year before, and read the report's own limits before you rely on a small county's figure. To size a California market before you spend, compare one county's civil unlimited and limited filings with its neighbors': where filings run high for the population, there are more disputes looking for a lawyer, and where they fall from one fiscal year to the next, demand may be moving elsewhere.

datasets.title: Federal civil filings by nature of suit and district, 12-month periods since 2018
datasets.summary: How many civil cases were filed in each of the 94 U.S. district courts and nationwide, by nature of suit, from the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts' Statistical Tables for the Federal Judiciary: Table C-3 (the 94 districts by case type: contract, real property, torts, civil rights, prisoner petitions, labor, Social Security, intellectual property and more, U.S. cases and private cases) and Table C-2 (the nation by about 100 natures of suit, such as product liability, medical malpractice, employment, the Fair Labor Standards Act, ERISA and consumer credit, with the basis of jurisdiction). One record per district and case type for the latest 12 months, with the year before and the history of every earlier table, and one record per nature of suit nationwide. In every table the 94 districts add up exactly to the national Total row, every circuit adds up to its districts and every nature-of-suit group adds up to the rows under it. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where federal civil cases are filed and which kinds are growing. A filing is a civil case commenced in a district court in the 12-month period, so the counts show how much federal demand each case type has in each district; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer, and they leave out state courts. Prisoner petitions are kept apart from the injury, employment and consumer groups. Compare a district's count with the nation and with the year before, and read the flag on small counts before you rely on a percent change.

datasets.title: CFPB complaints about debt collection, credit reporting and debt management, by state and month
datasets.summary: Complaints that consumers filed with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) about debt collection, credit reporting and credit repair, and debt or credit management, counted by state, month, product and issue from January 2018, with the last 12 months set against the 12 before and per 100,000 residents. One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory for each of the three product groups, with the share of complaints the company answered on time and the issue people raised most. The counts come from the CFPB's own Consumer Complaint Database search API, as aggregates, so no complaint, narrative, company name or ZIP code is ever copied; for every month the issue counts add up to the bureau's own count for each product group. The bureau changed its credit-reporting product name twice; every name is combined into one group. Complaints are consumers' own reports, not findings of any violation.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where consumers report the most trouble with debt collectors, credit bureaus and debt-management firms, and how that has moved, before you plan marketing for a consumer-law practice. Look up your state: the record gives the last 12 months of complaints for one product group, the rate per 100,000 residents, the change from the 12 months before, the on-time response share, the most common issue and 36 monthly counts. Read the rate as how often people in a state file complaints, not how often a law is broken.

datasets.title: FTC Consumer Sentinel reports by state: fraud, identity theft and imposter scams, 2024 Data Book
datasets.summary: Reports that consumers made to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's Consumer Sentinel Network in 2024, by state, DC and Puerto Rico, from the FTC's Consumer Sentinel Network Data Book 2024. Four records per jurisdiction: fraud and other reports and identity theft reports (each with the count, the rate per 100,000 people and the FTC's rank among the 50 states), imposter-scam reports (the share of the state's reports that the FTC prints, with a count and a rate derived from it, flagged as rounded) and fraud reports with the share reporting a loss, the total dollars reported lost and the median loss. Four national records give the whole country. A report is what a consumer or partner told the FTC, not a finding; the state tables leave out reports from state-specific data contributors and reports with no state.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many fraud, identity-theft and imposter-scam reports each state's consumers send the FTC, and how a state compares per 100,000 people, before you plan consumer-protection or fraud-recovery marketing. Look up your state: the records give each count, rate and rank as the FTC prints them. The imposter-scam count is derived from a whole percent, so it is a rounded estimate and is flagged. A firm weighing a new fraud-recovery or identity-theft page can rank the states it is licensed in by reports per resident: a high rate with a small population can mean a crowded field of victims and few firms speaking to them, while the imposter-scam share hints at which story to lead the page with.

datasets.title: County income and migration from IRS tax returns
datasets.summary: Individual income tax returns, individuals, adjusted gross income, salaries and wages in every U.S. county for the latest tax year, with the change in income per return from the year before, and the returns and income that moved into and out of each county and state between two filing years, from the IRS Statistics of Income county and migration files. The IRS rounds county returns to the nearest 10 and withholds a migration flow under 20 returns; withheld cells are left empty and marked suppressed, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how much income a county has and how fast it is moving, and where income is arriving from or leaving to: returns and adjusted gross income per county, the change over a year, and net migration from other states. These are the denominators for estate planning, tax, real estate and business law practices. Pair it with the legal-need and law-offices datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, County income and migration from IRS tax returns, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752984, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). County income and migration from IRS tax returns (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752984
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are totals from filed individual tax returns, not a county's wealth, a person's income or a prediction of who needs a lawyer, and migration shows where filers' addresses changed, not why. Questions about taxes, estates or property are for a licensed attorney or tax professional.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Read from the IRS Statistics of Income all-returns county file and the county and state migration files, kept row for row; the IRS state rows are used as published and the US row is the sum of the states. A gate re-reads every record from the live files, checks that the eight AGI brackets add up to every all-returns row, that county AGI equals each state row, that national moves in equal moves out, and that 300 county pairs agree between the inflow and outflow files.

datasets.title: Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI)
datasets.summary: What police agencies reported to the FBI over the last five complete calendar years, for every state and for 2,981 counties, home to 96.5% of U.S. residents: violent crimes, property crimes, arrests for driving under the influence, all arrests, and, for states, arrests for drug abuse violations. County rows add up the agencies the FBI places in each county (a city police department, a sheriff's office, a campus force; an agency that serves several counties counts in the county of its headquarters); a row says how many agencies there are and what share of the county's residents they cover, because a month an agency did not report is counted as not reported, never as zero, and a year in which no agency of the county reported is not published. Rates are per 100,000 residents of the agencies that did report. State rows are the FBI's own state series; the county rows add up the agency-level answers, which can come to less than the state series where the FBI's state count includes reports its agency-level answers do not return. The United States row is the sum of the states. Only counts are published: no officer, victim, suspect or agency name.
datasets.uses: Use it to size criminal-defense and DUI work in the counties a firm serves: how many DUI and drug arrests agencies report there each year, how that compares with violent and property crime, how the rate per 100,000 residents compares with the state and the country, and how complete the reporting is. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county by name. These are what agencies reported to the FBI, not all crime: an arrest is not a conviction, and a county with low coverage is understated.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23772522, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Crime and arrests by county and state: violent and property crime, DUI and drug arrests (FBI) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23772522
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of crimes and arrests that police agencies reported to the FBI, kept for research and marketing planning. An arrest says an officer took someone into custody, not that a charge was filed or proved. Whether and how to defend a charge, and every deadline, are for the person's own counsel.

datasets.measurementTechnique: FBI Crime Data Explorer monthly counts for every agency the FBI lists in the 50 states and DC (violent-crime and property-crime offenses, DUI and all arrests) are summed by calendar year and placed in the county the agency lists, or, for an agency that lists several counties, the listed county that holds its headquarters (Census Bureau geocoder); a month an agency did not report is kept as not reported, and rates use the residents of the agencies that reported. State rows are the FBI's own state series: the county rows never exceed them, and the gap is printed by the release check; the FBI's national rate, scaled to the share of residents covered, is the second check on the total.

datasets.title: Federal criminal cases by offense and district (U.S. Courts Tables D-1, D-2 and D-3)
datasets.summary: Criminal defendants whose cases were opened in the 94 federal district courts, counted from the Statistical Tables for the Federal Judiciary that the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts publishes for each 12-month period ending June 30 and December 31. Each record gives one district, one state with more than one district, or the whole country, for one period: the defendants commenced (transfers between districts left out), split by offense into nineteen columns and ten offense groups, with drug, immigration (illegal reentry shown on its own), firearms, fraud, sex offenses and traffic picked out, the felony, Class A misdemeanor and petty-offense split from Table D-1, and the same period a year earlier. National records add Table D-2's detail of about a hundred offenses, from bank robbery and health-care fraud to drunk driving on federal land. Every period's districts add up to the national total printed by the Courts, and every district ties to Table D-1.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the federal criminal-defense market where a firm practises: how many people are charged in each federal district each year, with what (drug trafficking, illegal reentry, gun possession, fraud, child exploitation, traffic on federal land), how many face a felony, and whether the count is rising. Look up a state to get every district in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a district by name. Federal cases are a small share of all criminal cases, so read it alongside state court filings.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Federal criminal cases by offense and district (U.S. Courts Tables D-1, D-2 and D-3), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744206, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.measurementTechnique: The Courts' Excel files for Tables D-1, D-2 and D-3 are read with the standard library and parsed by their header labels. A period is published only when Table D-3's 94 districts add up to its Total row in every column, every circuit row equals its districts, every row's offense columns add up to its total, Table D-2's offense groups add up to its total and tie to Table D-3, and every district's Table D-3 total equals its Table D-1 defendants commenced minus transfers. Districts are keyed to the Probative crosswalks; the state or territory of the district is the lookup key.

datasets.title: Legal market crosswalks: practice areas, federal case codes, states, federal districts and counties
datasets.summary: The shared keys that join every Probative dataset. One record per practice area (our taxonomy of consumer and business practice areas, each linked to the FOLIO Area of Law class it matches, the federal nature-of-suit codes of its cases, the site's practice pages and the datasets that measure its demand, supply, rules and money), per federal nature-of-suit code, per state and territory (FIPS and postal codes, Census region and division, federal circuit and districts), per federal judicial district (our district key, the Federal Judicial Center code and the court's CM/ECF id), per county and county equivalent in the 50 states, DC and the territories (Puerto Rico's municipios and the county equivalents of Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa and Midway: FIPS code, the federal district and statutory division it belongs to, its metro or micro area and its Census population), per former county code older sources still use (with the current counties that took its area), and per documented source code that names a place under another key (EEOC's WQ for Wake Island) or is not a place at all (military mail, the freely associated states, the VA's unplaced addresses, U.S. Courts' outside-the-U.S. code). Every county's district is read from the statute and checked against the counties U.S. Courts lists under each district in its bankruptcy Table F-5A.
datasets.uses: Use it to join any two Probative datasets, or our data with your own: a county FIPS code gives the federal district whose filings and bankruptcy figures apply to it, a practice area gives the federal case codes and the datasets that measure it, and a district key gives the counties and population it covers. Agents can resolve a place or a practice to the right keys before calling any other Probative dataset.

datasets.title: Legal deserts: law offices and lawyers per resident in every U.S. county
datasets.summary: Which counties have few or no law offices for their residents, under two definitions shown side by side. Offices: private law-office establishments per 10,000 residents (BLS QCEW, latest quarter, 2025 population), flagged when under 1 or when there is none. Lawyers: where a state's own bar or court publishes a county count (California, New York, Mississippi, Illinois), lawyers per 1,000 residents, flagged when under 1, the threshold the American Bar Association used in 2020. Each county also shows the Census count of solo legal-services firms with no employees, and whether it is in a metropolitan area, a smaller city area or neither. State and national rows count the counties. Bar figures are county-by-status totals only; no lawyer is named.
datasets.uses: Find counties with no office, compare a county with its state, or count residents living in thin-coverage counties. Both definitions are counts and rates, not findings about access to justice: bar addresses of record are not where a lawyer practises, and a nearby county's offices may serve the county.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Legal deserts: law offices and lawyers per resident in every U.S. county, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23721430, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Legal deserts: law offices and lawyers per resident in every U.S. county (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23721430
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts and rates from government statistics and state bar or court registries, kept for marketing planning. A county with few offices is not a finding about anyone's access to a lawyer; bar addresses are not places of practice.

datasets.title: Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA)
datasets.summary: Adverse event reports the FDA received about medical devices, counted by device product code and calendar quarter from 2025 Q1: reports, deaths, injuries, malfunctions and other, for the 300 product codes with the most reports and for all devices together. Counted with the openFDA device event API (licence CC0); no report row, narrative, patient or manufacturer is ever read, only counts. Reports are filed up to weeks after an event and are driven by litigation and recalls as well as by harm, so a count is not an incidence rate.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which device types draw the most adverse event reports and how that moves quarter to quarter: a sudden jump in injury reports for one product code is often the first public sign of a recall or a mass tort. Product-liability and mass-tort practices can watch the codes behind the devices they litigate. Pair it with the mdl dataset. Agents can look up the national total or a product code, compare quarters, or search a device by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752988, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Medical device adverse event reports by product code and quarter (FDA MAUDE via openFDA) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752988
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. A report to the FDA is an allegation that a device may have caused or contributed to an event, not a finding that it did, and a count of reports is not an incidence rate or proof of a defect. Questions about an injury from a medical device are for a licensed product-liability attorney and the person's doctor.

datasets.title: Social Security disability hearing waits and workloads by hearing office
datasets.summary: How long Social Security disability claimants wait for a hearing before an administrative law judge, office by office, from the Social Security Administration's own public data files: the average months from the hearing request to the hearing for cases closed in the month, and each hearing office's fiscal-year-to-date receipts, dispositions, cases pending and average days from request to decision, with SSA's rank among 159 offices. Each record is one hearing office, with the state it sits in. Counts and averages only: no judge, claimant, lawyer or firm is named.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how long SSDI and SSI claimants in a market wait for a hearing, and how loaded the local hearing office is, before you plan disability intake and advertising there. A long wait means more claimants still looking for representation and a longer time before a fee is paid. Compare an office with the national median and with its neighbors. The averages are SSA's own; they describe cases already closed, not how long a new claimant will wait.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Social Security disability hearing waits and workloads by hearing office, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741884, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Social Security disability hearing waits and workloads by hearing office (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741884
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are the Social Security Administration's published hearing-office statistics, kept for marketing planning. An average wait describes cases already closed, not how long any claimant will wait. Check SSA's current reports.

datasets.measurementTechnique: SSA's three hearing-office tables (average wait until hearing held, hearing office workload, and average processing time ranking) are read logged out in a browser, because ssa.gov refuses scripts, and saved with a SHA-256 of the rows computed on ssa.gov. The build checks the hashes, joins the tables by office name, requires the workload and ranking tables to agree on every office's processing time and region, and assigns each office to a state from its name.

datasets.title: Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS)
datasets.summary: Adverse event reports about drugs that reached the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and are served by openFDA, received 2024Q3 to 2026Q2: 2,649,395 reports in all, 1,430,033 serious and 197,378 with a death outcome. One record per active ingredient for the 312 ingredients with the most reports plus every ingredient named in an open multidistrict litigation (31 of them tagged with their MDL numbers): reports that list the ingredient, how many were serious, how many reported a death outcome, the same counts for each of the last eight quarters, and the five most reported reactions. National, one shard. A report names a drug and an event; it does not show that the drug caused the event, and FAERS holds duplicates, follow-ups and reports from outside the United States.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which drugs generate the most serious adverse event reports, how fast reports about an ingredient are rising or falling by quarter, and which reactions are reported most often, next to the open product-liability dockets that name the ingredient. Agents can look up the national record, compare ingredients and search by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752994, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Serious drug adverse event reports by active ingredient (openFDA FAERS) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752994
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This is not medical advice either. A report in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System is not proof that a drug caused an event; reports come from patients, clinicians and manufacturers, can be duplicated and are not verified. Questions about a medicine are for a health professional, and questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Counted server-side on the openFDA drug adverse event API (api.fda.gov/drug/event.json): `count` on patient.drug.openfda.substance_name.exact by quarter of `receivedate` for all reports, serious reports (serious:1) and reports with a death outcome (seriousnessdeath:1), plus one count over the whole window and one per ingredient for its five most reported reactions. No report text or patient field is read. The window is the last eight complete quarters. An ingredient is counted once per report that lists it, whether as suspect, concomitant or interacting drug, in the name openFDA harmonizes it to (a salt form such as 'losartan potassium' is its own name; every name that is the ingredient plus only a salt word is kept). A gate asks openFDA for the all-drug totals again, checks that each ingredient's quarters add up to its window, and re-counts fifty random ingredient-period cells with a different query.

datasets.title: Employment discrimination charges to the EEOC, by state and basis, FY 2009 to FY 2025
datasets.summary: Charges of workplace discrimination received by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), by state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory, fiscal year and basis (race, sex, national origin, religion, color, retaliation, age, disability, equal pay, genetic information and pregnancy under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act), from the EEOC's Tables E1b and E1a. One record per jurisdiction and basis for the latest fiscal year, each with its count, its share of the state's charges, the rate per 100,000 private-sector workers (BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, from fiscal year 2014) and the whole FY 2009 to FY 2025 history. Counts the EEOC suppressed are left empty and flagged, never filled in. A charge can name more than one basis, so bases add up to more than the total, and charges filed only with a state or local fair-employment agency are not counted.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many discrimination charges reach the EEOC from a state, which bases are cited most, and how that has moved over the years, before you plan employment-law marketing. Look up your state: the records give each basis for the latest fiscal year, its share of the state's charges and the rate per 100,000 private-sector workers, with the history. Small counts are suppressed by the EEOC, and a state with its own fair-employment agency sends part of its charges there.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Employment discrimination charges to the EEOC, by state and basis, FY 2009 to FY 2025, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23733005, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Employment discrimination charges to the EEOC, by state and basis, FY 2009 to FY 2025 (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23733005
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of charges received by the EEOC, kept for marketing planning. A charge is an allegation, not a finding of discrimination, and the counts leave out charges filed only with state and local agencies. Deadlines and rights are for your own counsel.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Table E1b (charge receipts by state and basis, suppressed version) and Table E1a (national, by basis) are downloaded from eeoc.gov and read by machine, finding the header row by its text. Counts are kept exactly as the EEOC prints them, a '*' cell is recorded as suppressed and never filled in, and the Total row is checked against Table E1a and against the sum of the states. The rate divides by the BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages annual average private employment.

datasets.title: Eviction filings by county and year (LSC Civil Court Data Initiative)
datasets.summary: Eviction filings (cases) by county and month from the Legal Services Corporation's Civil Court Data Initiative Eviction Tracker, which collects residential eviction filings from state and local courts: 1,464 counties and 34 states and territories, January 2016 through September 2025. Each record carries the filings of every full calendar year the county reports, the last twelve months where all twelve are present, filings per 100 renter households, the poverty rate and the latest month against the county's own historical average. Counties carry the Census FIPS code. LSC's data are released under CC0 1.0. The states and territories in the file are the ones LSC reports; the US record totals a year or month only where every one of them reports it.
datasets.uses: Use it to size landlord-tenant and housing-defense work in the counties a firm serves: how many eviction cases are filed there, how that has moved over the years and through the pandemic, and how filings compare with the number of renter households. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Eviction filings by county and year (LSC Civil Court Data Initiative), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752996, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Eviction filings by county and year (LSC Civil Court Data Initiative) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23752996
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of eviction cases filed in court, kept for research and market sizing. A filing is not an eviction carried out, a finding against a tenant or a measure of need, and one household can be filed against more than once. Questions about an eviction are for a licensed attorney or a local legal aid office.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Read cell for cell from LSC's two monthly CSV downloads on civilcourtdata.lsc.gov (county and state), after checking that LSC's Terms of Use still dedicate the data to the public domain under CC0 1.0. County FIPS codes are checked against the shared crosswalks (Connecticut's eight retired counties keep their old codes). A calendar year is shown only when all twelve months are in LSC's file; a missing month is never filled in. A gate downloads both files again and re-parses every cell with a separate reader, checks that counties add up to no more than their state, ties the monthly state file to LSC's weekly state file, and re-reads fifty random county-months.

datasets.title: Fatal crashes by county and type: trucks, motorcycles, pedestrians and bicyclists, NHTSA FARS 2019 to 2024
datasets.summary: Fatal motor-vehicle crashes in every US county, state and the nation for 2019 to 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS). One record per county, state and the US: fatal crashes and deaths in the newest year, the crashes that involved a large truck, a motorcycle, a pedestrian or a bicyclist, the pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists killed, alcohol-impaired, speeding and work-zone crashes, rural and urban roads, deaths per 100,000 residents, and every earlier year. Every county-year equals the accident table's own rows, and the counties add up to the state and the state to the nation. 2019 to 2023 are NHTSA's final files; 2024 is its first (annual report) release. The county-by-year table is at /research/fatal-crashes-by-county/data.csv. Counts only.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where fatal crashes concentrate, which counties have the most large-truck, motorcycle, pedestrian or bicyclist deaths, and how rural and urban counties compare per 100,000 residents. Look up a county by its 5-digit FIPS code. It counts crashes, not injuries or claims, and says nothing about fault.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Fatal crashes by county and type: trucks, motorcycles, pedestrians and bicyclists, NHTSA FARS 2019 to 2024, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23733739, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts from NHTSA's public crash census, kept for marketing planning. A county's count says nothing about who was at fault, and the newest year can change when NHTSA issues its final file.

datasets.title: Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center)
datasets.summary: How many federal civil lawsuits are filed in each U.S. county, and of what kind, over the last ten complete federal fiscal years, from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB). A case is counted in the county where the first-listed plaintiff lives (the first-listed defendant's county when the United States sues; the tract's county in land condemnation cases), by 16 nature-of-suit groups plus multidistrict litigations (MDLs), and rolled up to Probative's practice areas. One record per county carries all ten years, the prior-year change and the year-by-year history. Cases that cannot be placed in a county are published as rows of their own, per state and nationally: plaintiffs who live in the U.S. outside the court's state (with the MDL share), plaintiffs who live abroad, cases under a retired county code, and cases with an unrecorded county; district records add the same parts for each of the 94 district courts. Every state equals the sum of its counties and these rows, and the national total ties to the U.S. Courts' Table C-2 within a fraction of a percent. Only counts are published: no party, docket number or judge.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where federal civil litigation comes from: which counties send the most injury, employment, civil rights, consumer or Social Security cases to federal court, and how that moves year to year. County means where the plaintiff lives, not where the case is heard, so a county with no federal courthouse still has cases. Read the out-of-state, outside-U.S. and retired-code rows before comparing a state or district: in some years one mass-tort docket makes up most of the out-of-state cases. These are federal filings only, and state courts hear most lawsuits.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23750628, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Federal civil cases filed, by county of the plaintiff's residence, case type and year (Federal Judicial Center) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23750628
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of federal civil case filings from court records, kept for research and marketing planning. A filing says where a plaintiff lives and what kind of case was brought, not that a claim has merit, that a lawyer was hired or how a case ended. County means the county of residence of the first-listed plaintiff (the first-listed defendant's county when the United States sues; the tract's county in land condemnation cases), as the Federal Judicial Center codes it; the court also has codes for a plaintiff who lives in the U.S. outside the court's state and for one who lives abroad. Rights and deadlines in a matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.mcpLine: Federal civil cases filed by plaintiff county, state, district and case type, ten years, with out-of-state totals.
datasets.measurementTechnique: The Federal Judicial Center's civil Integrated Database file (cv88on) is streamed and counted in memory by machine: cases filed per federal fiscal year (October to September, by filing date), per COUNTY code (the county of residence of the first-listed plaintiff), per nature-of-suit code, with cases that carry a multidistrict litigation docket number counted as their own group. County codes are matched to the shared county list; a retired code with one successor goes to that county, one with several is shown as a former county, codes in no list as unrecorded, and codes 88888 and 99999 as out of state and outside the U.S. Nature-of-suit codes are grouped and rolled up to practice areas through the crosswalks. No party name, docket number or judge is read. The totals gate re-adds every state from its counties and these rows, and the U.S. Courts' Table C-2 (national) and Table C-3 (by district) are the second sources.

datasets.title: US law firm websites: practices, Spanish, intake, by state, county and practice area
datasets.summary: US law firms, state by state and county by county, from two kinds of open source: law firms' own public websites, read politely each week (robots.txt obeyed, a few pages per firm), and official state registries published as open data for reuse (New York's attorney registrations and business entities, and the business registries of Colorado, Oregon, Connecticut, Texas and Pennsylvania). For each state, county and practice area we count the firms found, how many have a website we read, and, of those websites, the shares that show Spanish-language pages, a 24/7 intake statement, a free consultation or no fee unless they win, a chat or online booking tool, legal structured data (schema.org LegalService or Attorney), review markup or an llms.txt file, with the median number of pages a firm has about the practice. Every row gives two coverage measures: the firms found against the employer law offices the Census Bureau's County Business Patterns counts, and the websites read against our estimate of the law firms with a website. A state is called a census only when the first reaches 0.70; until then the rows are a sample. These counts are CC BY 4.0. The firm-level rows behind them (name as the firm or registry gives it, offices by county and the yes-or-no facts, each linked to the page it was read on with the date) are published separately under the Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0, because the list of sites comes partly from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors), and are shown on the /firms/ pages. No firm is rated, scored or ranked, and no individual lawyer's data is published. Website sources: Common Crawl (its web graph and the Web Data Commons structured-data extract), OpenStreetMap and Wikidata.
datasets.uses: Use it to see the supply side of a local legal market next to its demand: how many firms in a county advertise divorce, immigration or car-accident work, and how many of their websites offer Spanish pages or say they answer around the clock. Read the two coverage measures first: where they are low, compare shares rather than totals. Look up a state for every county and practice row in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county or a practice. Firm-by-firm facts are on the /firms/ pages and in the ODbL downloads.

These are counts of facts read from law firms' own public websites and from official open registries on the dates shown, kept for research and marketing planning. Each row's two coverage measures say how much of the market it reaches. The counts describe what websites and registries say, not the quality of any firm or lawyer. datasets.measurementTechnique: Website firms: candidate sites from Common Crawl's web graph (registered domains with a law-firm term, five recent quarterly graphs, deduplicated), the Web Data Commons schema.org extract of Common Crawl, OpenStreetMap and Wikidata; a polite crawler reads each site (robots.txt first and obeyed, crawl-delay honoured with a 5-second floor per site, one request at a time per site, at most 11 requests per firm and 2 for a site that is not a US law firm; descriptive user agent; no logins, forms, JavaScript or challenge pages) and extracts facts by fixed rules. Registry firms: law-firm entities (names carrying a law-firm signal, active status) from state open-data portals read through their open APIs, matched to website firms by name and ZIP code. Offices are placed in counties with HUD's USPS ZIP-county crosswalk. Every count is re-derived from the firm rows in the release check; a re-crawl of 50 firms measures agreement; coverage (b) compares firms found with Census County Business Patterns 2023 employer law offices (NAICS 541110), coverage (a) compares websites read with a capture-recapture estimate of firm websites (OpenStreetMap vs Common Crawl lists).

datasets.title: New green cards (lawful permanent residents) by county, country of birth and class of admission
datasets.summary: New lawful permanent residents (green card holders) in the 200 U.S. counties with the most, for the two latest fiscal years: admissions by class (immediate relatives, family preference, employment preference, diversity, refugee and asylee adjustments, other) and the ten countries of birth with the most, with state sums set against the Yearbook of Immigration Statistics state totals. Read from the Department of Homeland Security's county workbooks, in which every cell is rounded to the nearest 10; sums are of rounded cells and understate the true figures, and the share of each state's total they cover is given.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where new permanent residents settle and from where: which counties receive the most green card holders, whether they come through family, employment, diversity or humanitarian routes, and which countries of birth lead. An immigration practice can size family-based, employment-based and naturalization demand by county. Pair it with the legal-need and uscis-offices datasets by state or county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its listed counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.title: How long federal civil cases take: outcomes, class actions and pro se share by district, nature of suit and year
datasets.summary: Federal civil cases from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB), counted by district, nature-of-suit group and fiscal year: cases filed, the share alleging a class action, the share with a pro se plaintiff, cases terminated, the median days from filing to disposition, the trial share, the median days to trial, and how terminated cases ended (settled, voluntarily dismissed, dismissed, default or consent, motion, trial, other, moved out). One record per district and group for the latest three fiscal years, each with its yearly series, plus a national record per nature-of-suit code. Only aggregates are published: no case-level row, party, docket number or judge. Filings re-add to the U.S. Courts' own totals within half a percent.
datasets.uses: Compare how quickly one district disposes of a type of civil case with the rest of the country, or how often a type of suit is filed as a class action or without a lawyer. These are court-wide medians for groups of cases; one case can take far longer or shorter.

datasets.title: Immigration court backlog, representation and asylum outcomes (EOIR workload statistics and case data)
datasets.summary: The size and movement of the U.S. immigration court backlog, from the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR). National series from EOIR's workload and adjudication statistics: pending cases, new cases, completions, the share of completed cases with a representative on record, asylum decisions and the share of grants among grants and denials, asylum applications pending and pending cases of unaccompanied children, by fiscal year. Pending proceedings by immigration court, by the respondent's state of address and by nationality, counted from EOIR's monthly FOIA case-data file, with the share that has a representative of record. Counts only: no case row, name or address is published, and every cell under 11 is suppressed. Every national table is re-added against its own totals row; the case-data counts are shown beside the published totals and never spliced into them.
datasets.uses: Use it to put the immigration court backlog and its representation rate on the record before you plan marketing, intake or staffing in a state. Look up US for the national series, or a two-letter state code for the pending proceedings of respondents with an address there and the immigration courts located in the state. EOIR says its statistics are subject to change, and the case-data counts are not the published backlog total, so quote the national series for the backlog and the case-data counts for where it sits.

datasets.title: Spanish-speaking demand vs Spanish-speaking lawyer supply, by state and metro
datasets.summary: How many people who speak Spanish at home, and how many who speak English less than very well, there are for each lawyer who speaks Spanish at home: for the US, every state and DC, and every metro area. Computed from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (2020 to 2024 five-year tables and microdata), each figure with its 90% margin of error and a reliability flag; estimates too unreliable to publish are withheld. Aggregates only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to decide where Spanish-language marketing is worth the effort. Look up your state or metro: the record gives how many residents speak Spanish at home and speak English less than very well, how many lawyers and judges speak Spanish at home, and the ratio between them, each with its margin of error. Where the sample is too thin, the number is withheld rather than guessed. Pair it with your own intake: if Spanish callers already reach you, the gap in your area tells you how much more demand is waiting. For intake staffing, compare the gap in a metro with the bilingual staff you already have: where Spanish-dominant residents far outnumber Spanish-speaking lawyers, a Spanish-answered phone line and Spanish landing pages tend to be the first fix, before any extra ad spend.

datasets.title: Law firm size, solos and receipts, by state: Census SUSB 2022, Nonemployer Statistics 2024 and Economic Census 2022
datasets.summary: How big U.S. law firms are and what they take in, for the US, every state and DC, from three Census Bureau sources. Employer law firms (NAICS 541110, offices of lawyers) by number of employees (fewer than 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 99, 100 to 499, 500 or more) with their employees, payroll and receipts, from the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) 2022. Businesses with no employees (mostly sole practitioners) and their receipts, by legal form, from Nonemployer Statistics 2024, which publishes legal services (NAICS 5411) as one group. Firm counts, receipts, the share of receipts held by the largest firms and firms by receipts size from the Economic Census 2022. One record per jurisdiction and class. Every size-class row adds up to its total row; classes the Census Bureau does not publish are left empty and flagged, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many law firms in a state are small, how much they take in, and how many solo practitioners sit outside the employer counts, before you plan marketing for a solo or small firm. Look up your state: the records give each size class with its share of firms and of receipts, the solo (nonemployer) count and receipts per solo, and the Economic Census cross-check. The sources cover different years (2022, 2024, 2022), and a firm with offices in several states is counted in each, so compare shares within a state or the US, not state counts added together.

datasets.summary: Private offices of lawyers (NAICS 541110) in every U.S. county, every state and the nation. For each area: establishments, March employment and average weekly pay from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (the latest quarter, with the seven before it); employer offices from the Census Bureau's County Business Patterns 2023 exactly as first published; firms with no employees in legal services from Nonemployer Statistics 2024; and the 2025 Census population estimate, so each area has offices and solo firms per 10,000 residents. datasets.title: Lawyer, paralegal and legal-staff pay by state and metro (BLS OEWS)
datasets.summary: How many lawyers, paralegals and legal assistants work in the US, in each state and DC, and in the larger metro areas, and what they are paid: the mean annual wage, the median and the 10th, 25th, 75th and 90th percentile wages, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) survey, May 2025. Every figure carries its BLS series id; figures BLS does not release are marked suppressed and never filled in. OEWS counts employees only: it leaves out owners, partners and the self-employed, so it is not what a firm's owners earn.
datasets.uses: Use it to price a hire or an in-house team against the local market, or to see where legal staff are paid most. Look up your state or metro: each record gives the employment and the mean annual wage for lawyers and for paralegals and legal assistants (and, for the US and states, legal secretaries and judicial law clerks), so you can compare staff cost with lawyer pay in the same place. When opening a second office, set the two metros side by side: the paralegal wage shows what intake and case-support staff will cost there, and the lawyer wage shows what a lateral hire expects, so the staffing line of the budget comes from the local market rather than from your home city.

datasets.title: Legal need by county: who may need a lawyer, from the American Community Survey
datasets.summary: The people in every U.S. county who may need a lawyer, counted from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2020 to 2024 5-year estimates: residents aged 65 and over, residents who are not U.S. citizens, foreign-born residents who arrived since 2010, residents who speak English less than very well (and Spanish speakers among them), divorced residents (and, for states, people divorced in the last year), veterans and veterans with a VA disability rating, residents with a disability, households on SSI, renter households and renters paying 30 or 50 percent of income on rent, residents without health insurance, workers who drive to work and median household income. One record per county (3,144, in the 50 states and DC), per state and for the US, each measure with its 90% margin of error and its share of the population it is counted in.
datasets.uses: Use it as the denominator of a local market: how many people in a county could need an immigration, family, elder-law, estate-planning, veterans' disability, Social Security disability, landlord-tenant or injury lawyer, and how that compares with the state. Pair it with the law-offices, deserts, fatal-crashes or immigration-courts datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state's counties, compare states, or search a county by name and measure.

datasets.title: Legal-services prices and jobs, monthly (BLS CPI, PPI and CES)
datasets.summary: Month by month since 2017, what consumers pay for legal services (Consumer Price Index), what law offices receive for their work (Producer Price Index for offices of lawyers, overall and by type of work where BLS publishes it), and how many people work in legal services (Current Employment Statistics), each next to the all-items or services index where that helps. Every value is read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' own database with its series id, base period, and a preliminary flag while BLS may still revise it. The consumer index measures a basket item, not a law firm's billing rate. Counts and index values only.
datasets.uses: Use it to put a fee, a billing rate or a hiring plan against the official price record. Look up the consumer legal-services index, the producer price index for offices of lawyers, or legal-services employment; each series comes with its last 24 months and the year-over-year change. To adjust a fee from an earlier year to today's prices, use the legal inflation calculator. To test a fee you set years ago, read the consumer legal-services index for the month you set it and for the latest month: the ratio shows how far legal prices moved in between, and the producer series for law offices shows whether firms' billings moved faster or slower than what clients paid.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Legal-services prices and jobs, monthly (BLS CPI, PPI and CES), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734854, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Legal-services prices and jobs, monthly (BLS CPI, PPI and CES) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734854
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are price and employment statistics from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, kept for marketing planning. Index values are not a fee schedule, and BLS revises recent months.

datasets.title: Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage
datasets.summary: The filing deadline the statute sets for five kinds of civil claims in every US state and DC: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage. Each record gives the period in the statute's own words, the citation, a link to the state's official code site, a verbatim quote, and the date read; where the same text says so, it adds whether the period runs from discovery and any outer limit (statute of repose). Where the official code could not be read, a cell may come from a court opinion that quotes or applies the statute; it is marked S (secondary) and names the court, case and date. Cells with neither are marked U and left blank. No calculator and no deadline arithmetic: tolling and exceptions apply.
datasets.uses: Look up one state and claim type, then read the quoted statute and its exceptions before relying on it. For marketing pages and intake scripts that mention filing deadlines, cite the statute and link the official text, never a bare number.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage, version 1.1.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23743673, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage (Version 1.1.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23743673
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are the periods as each statute states them, read in the official code on the date shown. Tolling, discovery rules, notice-of-claim deadlines for claims against a government, minors' rules and other exceptions can shorten or lengthen the time to file, and statutes change. Check the statute and ask a lawyer licensed in the state before relying on a deadline.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Each cell is read in the state's official code (the legislature's or code revisor's site, or its official PDF) and quoted verbatim; a script re-fetches each page and checks the quote and the period words, and pages that refuse scripts are read in a browser and saved as excerpts. Where the official code is published only through a state-contracted publisher or names no period for the claim, a court opinion on a court's own site that quotes or applies the statute is used instead and marked S; cells with neither are marked U.

datasets.title: Mass-tort docket tracker, federal MDL pending actions by month since 2019
datasets.summary: Pending actions in every federal multidistrict litigation (MDL), from the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation's monthly 'Pending MDL Dockets by Actions Pending' reports. One record per docket: the court's docket title, the transferee district, the docket type, actions now pending, actions ever filed, the change over 12 months, the peak pending count, and the docket's monthly pending count since 2019. Version 1.1 adds the 14 MDLs the court closed between 2026-01-01 and 2026-10-01 (dateClosed set, the peak and last count from the monthly series) and the court's reports by district and by docket type, with monthly groupings of the series. Every report's rows add up exactly to the court's own totals row. The full monthly series, judge included, is at /data/v1/mdl/history/index.json (one CSV per year); the district, type and closed-MDL files are at /data/v1/mdl/reports/index.json. Counts and dates only.

datasets.title: Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations
datasets.summary: For every US county with a Medicare- or Medicaid-certified nursing home, every state and territory, and the US: how many certified nursing homes and beds there are, how many times the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) fined them in the last three years and for how many dollars, how often and for how many days it denied payment, and how many health citations inspectors wrote at the actual-harm level or worse (scope and severity G to L), at the immediate-jeopardy level (J to L) and under the abuse, neglect and exploitation tags (F600 to F610), plus the share of rated homes with one star overall. Built each month from the four CMS Provider Data Catalog files behind Care Compare. Counts only: no facility names, addresses or certification numbers, and no resident data (CMS publishes none).
datasets.uses: Use it to size the market for nursing home abuse and neglect cases county by county: where the homes and beds are, where CMS has fined homes and how much, and where inspectors found residents harmed or in immediate jeopardy. A county with many beds, large fines and a high share of one-star homes is where families are most likely to be looking for help. Read it beside the elder population and law-office counts before you decide where to advertise or open an office.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741901, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Nursing home fines and harm citations by county: CMS penalties, actual-harm, immediate-jeopardy and abuse citations (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741901
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. This is a count of public CMS inspection and penalty records, kept for marketing planning. A citation is an inspector's finding, not a court's; a fine can be reduced or withdrawn on appeal; and nothing here says any home or person did anything unlawful.

datasets.title: Attorneys registered with the New York courts, by county, status and year of admission (NYS Office of Court Administration)
datasets.summary: How many lawyers are on New York's official attorney registration list, county by county. For each of the 62 counties the file counts the attorneys whose office address is there by registration status (currently registered, inside the 30-day reregistration window, delinquent, resigned, deceased, disbarred or suspended, incapacitated), by decade of admission to the New York bar, and per 10,000 residents using the Census Bureau's county population estimate. Further records count registrations with an office in each other state or territory, registrations with no office address in the public file, and the four judicial departments of admission, and the state record carries the admission-year history. Only counts are published: no name, address, phone number, firm or registration number is read, because the pull asks the court's open data portal for server-side totals and never downloads rows. Counts of one to four in a disciplinary status or an admission decade are withheld. Every record adds up to the state, the state ties to the source's own row count, and the American Bar Association's 2025 count of New York resident active lawyers sits between the two bounds the file allows.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many lawyers already serve a New York county before choosing where to advertise: active attorneys per 10,000 residents, how many are newly admitted, and how many are no longer in practice (delinquent, resigned, deceased). A county here is where the attorney's office is, not where clients live, and a lawyer in New York City may serve clients across the state. More than a quarter of the active attorneys have no office address in the public file and another quarter list an office outside New York, so county totals count lawyers with a published New York office, not every New York license.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Attorneys registered with the New York courts, by county, status and year of admission (NYS Office of Court Administration), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753008, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Attorneys registered with the New York courts, by county, status and year of admission (NYS Office of Court Administration) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753008
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of attorney registrations from the New York court system's public registration file, kept for research and marketing planning. A registration status is the court's record, not a judgment of any lawyer's skill or standing beyond that record, and a county is the county of the office address the lawyer gave, not where the lawyer practises or where clients live. Rights and deadlines in a matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: New York workers' compensation claims by county and accident year
datasets.summary: Workers' compensation claims assembled by the New York State Workers' Compensation Board in every New York county, for each accident year from 2000: the number of claims, how many have an attorney or representative (count and share), how many are controverted, how many have had a hearing and how many hearings were held, and how many are classified permanent partial or permanent total disability or occupational disease. Built only from SoQL aggregates of the Board's 5.7-million-claim file on NY Open Data (no claim-level row is read), with every count of 1 to 10 claims suppressed.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the workers' compensation market in New York county by county: how many claims are assembled each year, how often injured workers are represented (a measure of how much of the market lawyers already serve), how many claims are fought, and how many reach hearings and permanent disability. Pair it with the work-injuries and law-offices datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up New York, compare years, or search a county by name.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of claims the Board assembled, not claims accepted or paid, and a share with an attorney says how often workers were represented, not whether they needed to be. Questions about a workers' compensation claim are for a licensed New York attorney or the Board.

datasets.title: Legal-marketing ethics opinions, 2004–2026
datasets.summary: An index of US state and ABA ethics opinions, committee guidelines and court rulings on lawyer advertising and marketing, from 2004 to 2026 (most from 2015 on, plus earlier landmarks): lead generators, pay-per-lead, reviews, testimonials, trade names, websites, social media, chatbots and AI tools, competitor keywords and more. Version 1.1 adds an AI sub-index: 14 AI opinions coded on six marketing questions (chatbot disclosure, AI-made ads, intake and solicitation, superiority claims, confidentiality in marketing tools, and fees). Each record gives the issuing body, number, date, topics, a one-sentence holding in our words, a practical step, whether it is still in force, the official link, an exact short quote and the date read. It is not the opinions' full text.
datasets.uses: Use it before you try a new kind of marketing. If you want to buy leads, pay a referral platform, quote a client review, run a chatbot or bid on a rival firm's name, search the index for that topic and your state first. You will see which committees have already answered the question, what they said in plain words, what step it points to, and whether the answer still stands. Then read the opinion itself through its official link before you rely on it. Typical questions it answers: can a firm pay a lead generator per lead or per signed case; may an ad quote a client's online review; may a firm buy a competitor's name as a search keyword; who is responsible when a chatbot on the firm's site answers a legal question; and whether a trade name or a website domain can imply a specialty. Each answer names the committee or court, the opinion number and its date, so a partner can hand the citation straight to counsel. Version 1.1 also answers a newer question: what has each bar said about AI in marketing? Filter to the topic "ai" to see the 14 AI opinions, and read the six coded fields to see which ones say anything about chatbots, AI-made ads, intake, superiority claims, confidentiality and fees.

datasets.title: Legal ad-platform policy tracker
datasets.summary: The ad-platform policies that affect US law-firm advertising on Google Ads, Google Local Services, YouTube, Microsoft Ads, Meta, LinkedIn and ChatGPT ads: what each rule says in plain English, what a firm should do about it, which practice areas it touches, when it took effect, and a dated log of changes. Each record quotes the platform's own policy or help page and gives the date it was read.
datasets.uses: Use it before a campaign goes live, or when an ad is suddenly disapproved. Look up the platform and your practice area: the record says what the policy asks in plain English, what to change in your account or your ads, and the date the rule began. The change log shows what moved since you last checked, so a rejection is easier to trace to the rule behind it. Every record links to the platform's own page, which is the wording that counts. Typical questions it answers: what Google Local Services Ads checks before the 'Google Verified' badge shows; which legal services need Google's legal-services certification; what Meta allows for lead forms and special ad categories; how Microsoft Advertising treats bail bonds or debt relief; and what the newer ChatGPT and AI-answer ad programs say about legal advertisers. Each record says which practice areas it touches, so a family-law or immigration firm can skip the rules that only bind injury firms.

datasets.title: Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices)
datasets.summary: Recalls announced by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) since 2010, counted for the whole period, for each recall year and for each of ten hazard classes (fire and burn, falls and tip-overs, laceration, choking and suffocation, ingestion, entrapment and pinch injuries, electric shock, poisoning and chemicals, crashes and collisions, drowning, plus a class for the rest). Each count comes with the number of recalls whose notice reports an injury and the number that report a death, parsed from the notice's own incident text, and with the units the notices give. A recall that names several hazards counts once in each class and once in the totals. The counts come from CPSC's recall API; no firm names, contacts or narratives are kept.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which product hazards drive recalls, how recall volume changes year to year, and how often a recall notice reports a harm, as context for product-liability work. Agents can read the records at one level (the whole period, each year or each hazard class), compare levels, or search by hazard or year.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23779145, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Consumer product recalls by year and hazard (CPSC recall notices) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23779145
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of recall notices published by the Consumer Product Safety Commission, kept for research and market sizing. A recall is not a finding that a product caused any harm to any person, and it says nothing about whether anyone has a claim; deadlines for injury claims differ by state. Questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.measurementTechnique: One request per calendar year to CPSC's keyless recall API; each notice is reduced to a parsed row (hazard classes by keyword rules on the notice's hazard text, injury and death flags from its incident text after removing sentences that say none was reported, and the stated unit count), then counted by year and by hazard class. A gate re-fetches 50 random notices live, re-derives the same row and compares, and checks that classes, years and the whole period tie.
