datasets.title: Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54)
datasets.summary: Railroad casualties, highway-rail grade crossing incidents and train accidents that railroads reported to the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), 2021 through July 2026, for 2,315 counties with at least one report, 50 states and the US: 41,307 casualties (5,136 deaths and 36,171 nonfatal injuries or illnesses) from Form 55a, split by who was hurt (railroad employee on duty or off duty, contractor or volunteer, passenger, trespasser, other non-trespasser), 12,345 crossing incidents with the people killed and injured (Form 57) and 14,018 rail equipment accidents (Form 54), with the casualty count of each incident year. FRA's county codes are Census FIPS codes; counties retired since keep their old code. Counts come from FRA's rolling six-year views on data.transportation.gov and are aggregated server-side; no narrative or person-level field is read.
datasets.uses: Use it to size railroad-injury and crossing-accident work in the counties a firm serves: how many railroad employees, passengers, trespassers and motorists were hurt or killed there, how crossing incidents compare with train accidents, and how a county compares with its state. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753016, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Railroad casualties and crossing incidents by county (FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753016
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of events railroads reported to the Federal Railroad Administration, kept for research and market sizing. A report is not a finding of fault, and it says nothing about whether anyone has a claim; a railroad employee's injury claim has its own federal rules and deadlines. Questions about an injury are for a licensed attorney.

datasets.mcpLine: Railroad casualties, crossing incidents and train accidents by county from FRA Forms 55a, 57 and 54, by who was hurt.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Aggregated server-side (SoQL group by state, county, incident year and person class) from three views on data.transportation.gov: Form 55a casualties (bx7m-yn3v), Form 57 highway-rail crossing incidents (uwah-u9bn) and Form 54 rail equipment accidents (jm8x-ccxs). The views cover six calendar years and roll forward: a year that leaves the view stays in the dataset as last read, and years still in the view are re-read every month because railroads can amend their reports for five years. County codes are padded to Census FIPS and checked against the shared crosswalks. A gate checks that the aggregates add up to the views' row counts, that counties add up to states and states to the US, compares every state with FRA's raw Form 55a and Form 57 source tables, and re-counts fifty random county-years from the live view.

datasets.title: Referral-fee and fee-splitting rules for lawyers, by state
datasets.summary: When lawyers in different firms may split a fee, and what a lawyer may pay for a referral, in every US state and DC. Each record gives the state's fee-division rule (ABA Model Rule 1.5(e) or its equivalent: the proportion or joint-responsibility test, how the client must agree, whether each share is disclosed, any cap) and its rule on paying for recommendations (Model Rule 7.2(b) or its equivalent: referral-service charges, reciprocal referral agreements, nominal gifts), each quoted from the official rules text with the date read. Cells we could not read at an official source are blank and marked U.
datasets.uses: Look up one state before you agree a co-counsel or referral split, or before you sign with a referral service or lead vendor. Read the quoted rule text, and the state's ethics opinions, before you rely on it: this is a marketing reference, not legal advice.

datasets.title: Unwanted-call and text-message complaints to the FCC, by state and month
datasets.summary: Complaints about unwanted calls, robocalls and telemarketing that people filed with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), counted by state, month, issue and method (text message, prerecorded voice, live voice and others) from January 2015, with the last 12 months set against the 12 before and per 100,000 residents. One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory for text-message complaints and one for phone-call complaints. The counts come from the FCC's open Consumer Complaints Data, grouped on the FCC's server so no complaint, caller number or free text is ever copied, and the state rows add up to a separate FCC-side count for every month. Complaints are self-reported and unverified, not findings of any violation.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where people report the most unwanted texts and calls, and how that has moved, before you plan texting or phone outreach. Look up your state: the record gives the last 12 months of text-message or phone-call complaints, the rate per 100,000 residents, the change from the 12 months before, and three years of monthly counts. Read the rate as how often people in a state file complaints, not how often calls are made; a few filers can move a small state.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of complaints people filed with the FCC, kept for marketing planning. A complaint is a report, not a finding that anyone broke a law, and no phone number or complaint text is published. Texting and calling rules (the TCPA and state laws) are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: State civil-rights agency complaints and charges: figures printed in state annual reports
datasets.summary: Complaint and charge counts that state civil-rights agencies print in their own annual reports or publish as open data, one row per figure with the document's URL and a verbatim quote: California Civil Rights Department (2024 intake forms and immediate right-to-sue requests), Illinois Department of Human Rights (charges received and employment charges in fiscal year 2024, charges docketed in 2025) and the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission (allegations in employment complaints, fiscal years 2021-22 to 2024-25 and the part of 2025-26 so far). Each quote is re-checked against the document, and each Pennsylvania figure against the portal's own aggregate. States that block the fetcher or publish no count are not included.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how much discrimination-complaint activity state agencies handle beyond the federal EEOC charges, and to quote a state's own figure with its source. datasets.title: State trial-court case filings by county, court level and case type: Texas, Washington, Maryland, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon and West Virginia
datasets.summary: How many cases are filed in state trial courts, by county, court level and case group, from each state court system's own published statistics. Texas (Office of Court Administration): district, constitutional county and statutory county courts, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25, with district-court filings by case type. Washington (Administrative Office of the Courts): superior courts (criminal, civil, domestic, probate, adoption and parentage, mental illness, juvenile dependency and offender) and district and municipal courts (traffic infractions, DUI, other traffic and non-traffic misdemeanors, civil protection orders, civil and small claims), calendar year 2025. Maryland (Judiciary data dashboard): circuit-court filings by case type (tort, contract, divorce, paternity, juvenile, felony and more) and District Court filings (landlord-tenant, civil, criminal, DUI, traffic citations, peace orders and domestic violence), fiscal years 2012 to 2025. Indiana (Office of Judicial Administration): circuit and superior court new filings by Rule 8 case type (felony, misdemeanor, tort, collection, small claims, eviction, foreclosure, domestic relations, estates, guardianship, juvenile), calendar year 2025 (provisional) beside 2024. Wisconsin (Director of State Courts Office): circuit-court cases opened by county and category (felony, misdemeanor, criminal traffic, traffic, civil, small claims, divorce, other family, paternity, adoption, estates and informal probate, guardianship, commitments, juvenile delinquency and child-welfare), 2020 to 2025. Virginia (Supreme Court of Virginia, Office of the Executive Secretary): circuit courts (domestic and family, felony, misdemeanor, general civil, probate, protective orders), general district courts (landlord-tenant, garnishment, civil, felony, misdemeanor, infractions, protective orders) and juvenile and domestic relations district courts (custody and visitation, child support, delinquency, child dependency, protective orders) by locality (county or independent city), calendar year 2025. Pennsylvania (Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts): courts of common pleas in all 67 counties, civil cases by case type (motor-vehicle and other torts, mass torts, medical malpractice, contract and debt collection, landlord-tenant, mortgage foreclosure) and new criminal, protection from abuse, spousal and child support, custody, divorce, juvenile dependency and delinquency, adoption and guardianship cases, calendar year 2024. Oregon (Oregon Judicial Department): circuit courts in all 36 counties (general civil, landlord-tenant, small claims, felony, misdemeanor, violations, divorce, other domestic relations, protective orders, juvenile, probate, civil commitment), calendar year 2025. West Virginia (Supreme Court of Appeals): circuit courts (general civil, felony, misdemeanor, adoption, guardianship, mental health, juvenile), family courts (divorce, domestic violence, other domestic relations) and magistrate courts (small claims, personal safety and domestic violence protective orders) in all 55 counties, calendar year 2025. Every record keeps the state's own category names and the numbers added into each group (components), and carries a harmonized group and the practice areas it bears on, so a county's filings can be read as demand for personal injury, family, landlord-tenant, small claims and debt, probate, criminal and DUI, juvenile and traffic work. In every source the counties add up to the state's own printed total where it prints one (Texas, Washington, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon, West Virginia), and the state rows for Maryland are the sum of the counties because the file prints no statewide row. Every record carries its FIPS code (the state's on a state row, the county's on a county row) so it joins Census and other county data. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is, county by county, for the states listed. A case filed is a new case (Texas counts new cases and motions added to the docket), so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Compare a county with its state row and with the year before. Read the court level: the same county can have several levels of court, and one level is not the county's total. The harmonized groups are our grouping of each state's own categories, and the state's category is always shown beside it. Compare a group across states with care: courts differ in what they hear, and in whether they count cases or incidents (Maryland counts traffic citations as incidents).
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, State trial-court case filings by county, court level and case type: Texas, Washington, Maryland, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon and West Virginia, version 1.4.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23777048, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). State trial-court case filings by county, court level and case type: Texas, Washington, Maryland, Indiana, Wisconsin, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Oregon and West Virginia (Version 1.4.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23777048
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts from each state court system's published statistics, kept for marketing planning. A case filed is a new case on a court's docket (in Texas, a new case or motion), not a person or a client. Check the state's current report.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Texas: the Office of Court Administration's county summary and district activity detail workbooks (Excel) are read by machine and quoted back as printed; a table counts only if the counties add up to the workbook's own statewide Total row in every column and the district Total rows equal the Activity Detail workbook. Other states: each state's published Excel or CSV file is read by machine, the state's categories are mapped to harmonized groups and the practice taxonomy with the original category and every component kept on the record, and a state counts only if its gates pass: Washington counties = the Statewide Total row in all columns, each county's categories = its Total Filings, limited-jurisdiction courts = their county rows = the statewide row; Indiana court rows = the workbook's STATE row in every case-type column and each row's case types = TOTAL; Wisconsin counties = the state's own Caseload Summary row in every category; Virginia: the three caseload PDFs (circuit, general district, juvenile and domestic relations) are read from the PDF text layer page by page, each month row must add to its printed year total, the localities must add to the printed Statewide row in every category and in total, every locality's categories to its printed Locale Total, and each circuit's or district's localities to its printed total; Pennsylvania: the statewide and 67 county caseload PDFs are read from the PDF text layer, in every county and statewide the 46 civil case types must add to the printed total docketed cases and to each of the seven printed section subtotals (all 476 of them, statewide and county), and the 67 counties must add to the statewide report in every civil case type and every new-case count; Oregon: the Cases Filed PDF, where the case types must add to their category and the categories to the printed total in every county, each district's counties to its printed total, and the 36 counties to the statewide table in every row; West Virginia: the annual statistics report's county tables, where the 55 counties must add to the printed Total row in every column; Maryland has no printed total so duplicates, blanks and county coverage are checked and the state row is the county sum. A failed gate writes nothing.

datasets.title: Toxic chemical releases by county (EPA Toxics Release Inventory)
datasets.summary: Toxic chemicals that industrial and federal facilities reported releasing on site to the Environmental Protection Agency's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) in reporting year 2024, for 2,437 counties with a reporting facility, 56 states and territories and the US: 21,482 facilities and 2,842,308,160 pounds in all (530,322,130 to air, 188,664,266 to water, 2,123,321,764 to land), with the pounds of known or suspected carcinogens, PFAS, ethylene oxide, benzene and lead, and the on-site total of each of the earlier years kept (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023). State records list the three largest parent companies. Counties carry the Census FIPS code. Dioxin-like compounds, which facilities report in grams, are converted to pounds. TRI counts reported releases by listed chemicals from covered facilities; it is not a measure of exposure or of harm.
datasets.uses: Use it to size toxic-exposure and environmental-injury work in the counties a firm serves: how many covered facilities release listed chemicals there, how many pounds, how much of it is carcinogens or PFAS, and how a county compares with its state and with earlier years. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.title: Truck and bus crashes by county, state and year (FMCSA crash file)
datasets.summary: Crashes involving a commercial truck or bus that states reported to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), counted from its Motor Carrier Management Information System (MCMIS) crash file for every county, state and territory and the US over the last ten complete calendar years. Each record gives, for the latest year, the crashes, the fatal crashes, the crashes with injuries, the crashes where a vehicle was towed away, the crashes involving a bus, the deaths and the injuries, with the whole ten-year history and the ten-year totals. A crash is one state crash report, counted once however many trucks and buses it involved, and its deaths and injuries are counted once. State records add the number of active carriers based in the state, from the FMCSA Company Census File. Counties with no reported crash are listed with zeros, and reports without a usable county code are kept in a 'county not given' row for their state, so counties always add up to the state.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the truck-accident market in the counties a firm serves: how many truck and bus crashes happen there each year, how many are fatal or cause injuries, and whether the count is rising. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county by name. It counts only federally reportable crashes, and some states report more completely than others, so read it alongside the fatal-crash census from NHTSA.

datasets.title: County and state unemployment: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics, annual averages and latest month
datasets.summary: The unemployment rate, number unemployed, employed and labor force for every county and state, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) program: the annual average for each year 2015 to 2025 and the latest 13 months. Each county and state record carries the latest annual average, the change from the year before and since 2015, and the latest month (preliminary until BLS revises it). County figures are model-based estimates that BLS controls to its state totals; the build checks that county employment, unemployment and labor force add up to the state's. Retired Alaska census-area codes with no current estimate are left out, and Connecticut appears as BLS publishes it.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how tight or slack the labor market is in the counties a firm serves, and where it is turning: rising unemployment is the backdrop to layoffs, wage disputes and unemployment-benefit appeals, and a county's rate against its state's shows where local conditions differ. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare up to ten states, or search by county name. These are survey-based model estimates, not a count of people, and the newest month is preliminary.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, County and state unemployment: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics, annual averages and latest month, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753061, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.title: USCIS naturalization and green card applications by field office
datasets.summary: Applications to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for naturalization (Form N-400, general and military) and for a green card by adjustment of status (Form I-485, family, employment, humanitarian and other), received, approved, denied and pending at every USCIS field office and service centre, for each fiscal quarter USCIS has published, with the nationwide totals. Read cell for cell from the agency's quarterly performance workbooks and tied to its service-wide quarterly totals. USCIS prints D where disclosure standards are not met; those cells are left empty and marked suppressed, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where naturalization and green card work is concentrated and where it waits: how many applications each USCIS office takes in, decides and has pending, and how the mix of family, employment and humanitarian green card cases differs by office. An immigration practice can compare the offices that serve its clients. Pair it with the legal-need and immigration-courts datasets by state. Agents can look up a state, compare up to ten states, or search an office by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, USCIS naturalization and green card applications by field office, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753086, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). USCIS naturalization and green card applications by field office (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753086
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of applications that USCIS received and decided at each office, not the outcome of any one case or a prediction of one: a pending count says how many applications are waiting, not how long yours will wait or where it will be decided. Questions about an immigration case are for a licensed immigration attorney or an accredited representative.

datasets.title: VA disability compensation recipients by county and combined rating
datasets.summary: Veterans receiving VA disability compensation in every U.S. county on September 30, 2025 (fiscal year 2025), from the Department of Veterans Affairs county file on data.va.gov: the total and the count in each combined service-connected rating band (0 to 20%, 30 to 40%, 50 to 60%, 70 to 90% and 100%), by age group (17 to 44, 45 to 64, 65 and over) and by sex, with the same county's total and 100% count a year earlier. One record per county (3,144, in the 50 states and DC), per state and DC (the sum of its counties), for Puerto Rico, for the other territories, for veterans paid abroad, for unknown addresses and for the US. Cells VA suppressed to protect privacy are left empty and marked suppressed, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to size a veterans' disability practice in the counties a firm serves: how many veterans already receive compensation there, how many have a low or middle rating and how many are already rated fully disabled, how fast the count is growing, and how a county compares with its state. Pair it with the law-offices or deserts datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.

datasets.title: VA disability compensation, pension and survivor dollars by county (VA GDX report)
datasets.summary: Dollars the Department of Veterans Affairs paid in direct benefits in fiscal year 2025 in every U.S. county, from the Geographic Distribution of VA Expenditures (GDX) workbook of VA's National Center for Veterans Analysis and Statistics: disability compensation and veterans pension, dependency and indemnity compensation (DIC) and survivors pension, insurance, and specially adapted housing, with the total recomputed as the sum of the four (the workbook's Total column is a formula), and the compensation, pension and survivor dollars of the year before for the change. One record per county or county equivalent (3,223), per state, DC, Puerto Rico and Guam, for foreign countries, the Freely Associated States, other U.S. territories and unknown addresses, and for the US (187,660,338,257 dollars in all). Counties carry the Census FIPS code; Connecticut's counties are the planning regions.
datasets.uses: Use it to size a veterans' disability practice by money, not headcount: how many dollars of compensation and survivor benefits reach a county every year, how fast that is growing, and how a county compares with its state. Pair it with the va-compensation dataset (recipients by rating) by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state and its counties, compare up to ten states, or search a county by name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, VA disability compensation, pension and survivor dollars by county (VA GDX report), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753088, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are dollars VA paid, placed by the address of the veteran or survivor receiving them; they are not claims, awards, backlogs or unmet need. Questions about a claim are for an accredited attorney, agent or veterans service officer.

keywords: VA pension and survivor benefits by county
datasets.measurementTechnique: Read from VA's GDX workbook for the fiscal year (and the year before) cell for cell: the 'County Direct Exp', 'State Direct Exp' and 'CD Direct Exp' sheets. The workbook's Total column is a formula, so the total in each record is recomputed as the sum of the four direct categories and checked against the workbook's cached value. County rows are matched to vintage-2025 county FIPS codes in the shared crosswalks by state and county name (Connecticut's eight retired counties are listed with no dollars and are left out; its planning regions carry them). A gate re-reads fifty counties from the live workbook with a separate reader, checks that counties add up to VA's state rows and states to its Grand total, ties the Congressional District sheet (a separate cut of the same dollars) to each state, and holds dollars per recipient against the va-compensation dataset.

datasets.title: Vehicle safety complaints by state, make and model year (NHTSA complaint file)
datasets.summary: Safety complaints about cars, trucks, SUVs, motorcycles and RVs that owners filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), counted from its Office of Defects Investigation complaint file for the ten most recent model years, by the complainant's state, the make, the model year and the part of the vehicle named (engine, brakes, air bags, steering and the other NHTSA component groups). Each record gives the complaints, how many report a crash, a fire, an injury or a death, the people reported injured and killed, the complaints filed in the last twelve months, and how many concern a make, model and year that has a safety recall (and a recall of the same system), joined from NHTSA's recall file. State records list every make; make records add the model year by component table and each model's counts; national make records add each model by model year and the number of recall campaigns. A complaint is counted once however many parts it names. Only counts are kept: no narrative, VIN, city, name or complaint number.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the lemon-law and vehicle product-liability market in the states a firm serves: how many owners there complain about each make and model year, which systems they name, how many complaints involve a crash, a fire or an injury, and how many concern vehicles that were recalled. Look up a state to get every make, compare up to ten states, or search for a make such as Ford or a model such as Wrangler. Complaints are unverified owner reports, so read them as a signal of where owners have trouble, not as proof of a defect.

datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Vehicle safety complaints by state, make and model year (NHTSA complaint file) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744214
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of unverified complaints that vehicle owners filed with NHTSA, kept for research and marketing planning. A complaint is not a finding that a vehicle is defective, and a count says nothing about whether any owner has a lemon-law or injury claim. Rights and deadlines are for your own counsel.

datasets.measurementTechnique: NHTSA's ODI complaint flat file (FLAT_CMPL.zip, one row per component a complaint names) is read in full each month; vehicle complaints for the ten most recent model years are counted once per ODI number by the complainant's state, make, model, model year and component group, with crash, fire, injury and death flags, and joined to the ODI recall file (FLAT_RCL_POST_2010.zip) by make, model and model year. datasets.title: VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation
datasets.summary: How many attorneys and claims agents the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs has accredited to help with benefit claims, counted by the state (and, in the county file, the county) of each person's business address, against the VA's own projection of living veterans (VetPop2023, rounded to the nearest 1,000). One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory, one for the United States and one for people whose list entry shows no US state, each with attorneys, claims agents, veterans per accredited attorney, accredited attorneys and agents per 100,000 veterans, the number accredited in the last 12 months and how many counties have none. Records for the Board of Veterans' Appeals add its decisions in fiscal year 2024 by outcome and by type of representative. The VA's lists name every person; only counts are read, and no name, phone number, registration number or ZIP code is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where VA-accredited attorneys and agents have offices compared with the veterans a state is projected to have, which counties have none, and how many were accredited recently, before you plan veterans' benefits marketing. Look up your state: the record gives the counts, the ratios and the history since this dataset began. The count is by business address, so it shows where offices are, not how many veterans each person serves, and the veteran counts are a projection.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740008, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of people on the VA's public accreditation lists and of Board of Veterans' Appeals decisions, kept for marketing planning. An accreditation is the VA's permission to help with claims, not an endorsement or a measure of quality, and the counts say nothing about any veteran's claim. Deadlines and fees are for your own counsel.

datasets.measurementTechnique: The VA Office of General Counsel's two complete lists (attorneys and claims agents) are downloaded with the same single form POST the page's Download button sends, parsed in memory and counted by the state in each business address, by county (the ZIP code's county in the Census ZCTA-to-county file) and by year accredited, then discarded; no name, phone, registration number or ZIP code is stored. Counts must add up to the lists' row counts, county counts to each state, and three states are matched against the VA's own search form. Veterans are VetPop2023 county rows (which add up to its state table) at the latest September 30, rounded to the nearest 1,000. The Board's table rows must add up to its grand total and its decision count.

datasets.title: Wage-and-hour and OSHA enforcement by county, state, act and industry (U.S. Department of Labor)
datasets.summary: What the U.S. Department of Labor found when it enforced wage and safety laws, counted for every county, state and territory and the US over the last ten complete federal fiscal years. From the Wage and Hour Division (WHD): concluded cases, cases with violations, back wages found owed, employees owed back wages, civil money penalties, Fair Labor Standards Act overtime and minimum wage back wages, and child labor violations. From the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), federal and state-plan offices: inspections (and how many followed a complaint, a referral, an accident or a fatality or catastrophe), violations cited (serious, willful, repeat), and penalties. State and US records add one record per law WHD enforces (FLSA, FMLA, Davis-Bacon, the Service Contract Act, H-2A, H-2B, H-1B, MSPA and others) and one per industry sector. Only counts and sums are published: no employer name, address or case number, and back wages are suppressed wherever 1 or 2 employees were owed.
datasets.uses: Use it to size wage-and-hour and workplace-safety work in the counties a firm serves: how often federal investigators find unpaid wages there, how much is owed and to how many workers, which laws and industries the cases come from, and how many OSHA inspections follow a complaint, an accident or a death. Look up a state to get every county, law and industry in it, compare up to ten states, or search for a county or an industry by name. These are the cases the federal government closed, not all wage theft or workplace injury: state labor agencies and private lawsuits are not in it.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Wage-and-hour and OSHA enforcement by county, state, act and industry (U.S. Department of Labor), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744226, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts and sums of federal enforcement findings, kept for research and marketing planning. A WHD back-wage finding or an OSHA citation is the agency's finding, not a court judgment, and employers can contest them. Rights and deadlines in a wage or injury matter are for your own counsel.

datasets.title: WARN Act layoff and closure notices by county: California and Texas
datasets.summary: How many mass-layoff and plant-closure notices employers filed under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act, and how many employees they covered, for every county in the states whose workforce agencies publish the notices as files: California (July 2023 on, from the Employment Development Department's reports) and Texas (2019 on, from the Texas Workforce Commission's open-data table). Each county, state and county-not-given record carries the last 12 months, the last complete calendar year, the total since the file starts, and the month-by-month series. Only counts are kept: no employer name, address or contact. Notices are dated by the day the state agency received them. Other states are not included.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where layoffs are being announced: counties with a run of large notices have workers who may need an employment lawyer (final pay, severance, WARN notice-period claims, unemployment appeals), and a county with none is not necessarily quiet, because the file covers only two states and only employers large enough to be covered. Look up a state to get every county in it, compare the two states, or search by county name.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, WARN Act layoff and closure notices by county: California and Texas, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753097, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). WARN Act layoff and closure notices by county: California and Texas (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23753097
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of notices employers filed with state agencies, kept for research and marketing planning. A notice is a plan, not a layoff that has happened, and says nothing about whether any worker has a legal claim; rights and deadlines are for your own counsel.

No employer-level data is stored.

datasets.title: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI)
datasets.summary: How often workers are hurt on the job in each state and industry, and how many die: the nonfatal injury and illness rate per 100 full-time workers for private-industry sectors and detailed industries in the states BLS publishes (Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses, 2024), and the number and rate of fatal work injuries in every state and DC, with the major cause and the industry rate (Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024). Every record carries its BLS series or table. Survey estimates carry a relative standard error and a noise flag; figures BLS does not publish are marked suppressed and never filled in. It is statistics about industries and states, never about a named employer.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which industries hurt workers most in a state, how a state's injury rate and fatal-injury rate compare with the nation, and what causes the deaths. Look up a state: each record gives the rate, the count, how precise the estimate is and the year-by-year trend where BLS publishes one. These are rates for whole industries, not for any one workplace, so they do not say whether a particular injury is covered by workers' compensation.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740010, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI) (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740010
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are survey and census statistics from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, kept for planning. A rate describes a whole industry in a state, not any one employer, and it does not say whether anyone has a workers' compensation claim.

datasets.mcpLine: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry, from BLS SOII and CFOI: rates, case counts and the riskiest sectors.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Nonfatal rates and case counts are read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII) time series IS by series id: total recordable cases, private industry, by state and industry, with the relative standard error. Fatal injury counts, causes and rates are read from the Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI) state tables. Cells BLS does not publish are recorded as suppressed with no value. Nothing is imputed and no employer is named.
